paras: The Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man took place in Nashville, Tennessee, on a Tuesday in mid-February 1882, apparently February 14, when a policeman fired at a man running from him. The bullet missed, and no one was hurt. The Memphis Daily Appeal noted the incident chiefly to remark that an officer who killed a fleeing person who was not a felon could be prosecuted for murder.

According to the Memphis Daily Appeal, a Nashville policeman shot at a "fleeing negro" on Tuesday, and the bullet "missed its mark." The paper named neither the officer nor the man, called the latter only "the suspected person," and did not say what he was suspected of or why he ran. Nor did it give the time of day, the street or place, or whether the man was later caught.
No report of an arrest, a complaint against the officer, or any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The only known account is a two-sentence item in the "Tennessee News" column of the Memphis Daily Appeal of February 18, 1882, printed among notes on town incorporation, crops, the state treasury and items from other Tennessee papers. The column said the miss was fortunate "for both the officer and the suspected person" and treated the shooting as an occasion for a point of law. Had the officer killed the man, it observed, he would have been liable to prosecution for murder, because courts had held that "an officer has no right to fire at an escaping person, unless he be a felon."

The item identified the man only by race, using the word "negro," and made no further comment on the officer's conduct. No other report of the shooting, in Tennessee or elsewhere, appears in the coverage.
